Introduce yourself and KAVACH. The project connects login events to security alerts and makes the underlying evidence available during an investigation.

Project source: Thesis metadata.tex.

A failed login has several possible causes
It could be a mistyped password or one attempt in a larger pattern.
Context helps decide what warrants attention
Time, IP, device and recent activity show what changed.
Users see their own activity. Administrators can investigate alerts and respond.

Start with a simple example. A failed password might be a typo. Repeated failures or a sudden change in device give the administrator more context about what to investigate.

Deterministic detection runs in the application. PostgreSQL holds the evidence used for investigation.

Walk from left to right. React is the interface. Spring Boot checks permissions and runs the application logic. PostgreSQL stores the evidence. Grok or the fallback planner can assist when someone asks a question.

title: From sign-in to a risk score

text: From sign-in to a risk score
One login event can trigger several rules.
Check the account and verify its password.
Save the outcome, time, IP and device.
Check six rules and store each match.
Sum the account’s recent rule weights.
Known-account login failures are recorded in a separate transaction. Unknown usernames leave an audit record.

Follow a single sign-in. Spring Boot checks the credentials, attempts to store the event and evaluates the rules. Saving telemetry in a separate transaction helps preserve evidence when authentication fails.

Each matching rule adds a fixed weight to the account’s recent risk score.
A login event is marked failed.
A login happens between midnight and 04:59.
An inactive account attempts to sign in.
The account has history and the IP is unfamiliar.
The account has history and the device is unfamiliar.
At least five failures meet the 10-minute check.

Use one rule to illustrate the table, such as a new IP adding 40 points. Multiple rules can match the same event. The severity shown here belongs to the rule match.

Project source: KAVACH thesis chapters 3–5 and backend implementation.
Slide style adapted from Opportunity Engine, supplied Canva reference.
Add the weights of alerts detected in the last 24 hours. Cap the score at 100.
Illustrative calculation. A score of 90 places the account in the Critical tier.

Read the example aloud. Twenty plus forty plus thirty equals ninety, so the account is Critical. Older alerts stop contributing after 24 hours. The weights are fixed priorities.

An administrator can ask for an explanation or a summary of recent anomalies.
Request a summary of recent alerts.
Query authorized login and anomaly records.
Show the findings with a record of the tools used.
Grok can guide the investigation. A deterministic fallback is available if live inference fails.

Use the example prompt ‘Summarize recent alerts.’ The assistant can query authorized records and show its tool steps. In the implementation, the outer loop handles supplied follow-ups and the inner loop handles tool calls.

title: What users and administrators can do

text: What users and administrators can do
Access depends on the caller’s role and the account being reviewed.
Inspect alerts linked to their account
Review the dashboard and investigation evidence
Deactivate or reactivate accounts as needed
Review the audit trail for account actions

A user sees their own activity. Administrators can review across accounts and decide whether to change account status. The backend checks authorization and records administrative actions.
